questions.stem: Describe the riskiest assumption.
options: The assumption that is both most uncertain and most damaging if wrong
The cheapest assumption to test, because a cheap test gives the fastest learning
The assumption the client dislikes most, because it is the one they will challenge
The first assumption listed, because the group writes the most important one first
questions.why: Test the one in the bottom-right cell first. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify the two questions used to find the riskiest assumption.
options: How sure are we? What happens if we are wrong?
How much does it cost to test? Who owns the assumption?
Is it new to the organisation? Is it popular with the staff?
When did we first make it? Where in the plan does it appear?
questions.why: List every assumption and ask both. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Describe what to do with an assumption you are confident about whose failure would be fatal.
options: Test it cheaply — confidence is not evidence
Skip it, because the team's confidence shows that it has already been checked
Note it and move on, because confident assumptions do not need testing
Decide and watch it, because the damage will be visible early enough to act
questions.why: Confidence is not evidence. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Describe what to do with an assumption you are unsure about whose failure would be small.
options: Decide and watch it
Test it first, because uncertainty always needs evidence before action
Abandon the plan, because an uncertain assumption makes the plan unsafe
Run a pilot, because a pilot is the only way to settle an uncertain assumption
questions.why: Unsure + small damage: decide and watch. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify what the riskiest assumption is almost always about.
options: People — that they will change a habit, use a new system, or say what they actually do
Money — that the budget will be approved and the costs will not rise
Technology — that the new system will work with the old one
The weather — that conditions will stay as they were during planning
questions.why: Almost always about people. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Identify the three conditions that make something a test rather than a demonstration.
options: One question; a threshold set before; a result that would stop you
A budget; a date; a sponsor who will defend the result
Many questions; a survey of users; a written report
Approval from the manager; applause from the team; a slide for the client
questions.why: Most student 'testing' fails all three. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Explain why a test that cannot come out badly is not a test.
options: It is a demonstration — nothing it shows could change your mind
Tests must be expensive, or the result will not be taken seriously
Tests must take at least a month to produce reliable data
Tests need many questions to cover every aspect of the idea
questions.why: If no outcome would change your mind, you are seeking approval. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Identify what to watch in a test.
options: What people DO, not what they say they would do
What people say when asked directly about the idea
What managers predict customers will do
What the supplier promises the system will achieve
questions.why: Stated intention is the weakest evidence in business. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Describe the classic bad test.
options: Asking colleagues whether your idea is good
Watching customers for a day without telling them what you are testing
A one-counter trial in a single branch on a single day
A paper mock-up shown to real users before anything is built
questions.why: They are not the customer, they want to be kind, and nothing they say could stop you. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Explain how the threshold must be written.
options: Before the test, as a number, where others can see it — 'proceed if at least 12 of 40 do X'
After the result is in, so that the threshold reflects what was actually possible
As an adjective — 'proceed if the response is strong' — so that judgement is kept
Privately, so that the team is not influenced by knowing the target during the test
questions.why: Set BEFORE, in numbers. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Identify the five rungs of the test ladder in order.
options: Ask five people; watch them; paper version; one-day trial; pilot
Pilot; one-day trial; paper version; watch them; ask five people
Survey; focus group; launch; review; relaunch
Idea; plan; budget; build; sell
questions.why: Each rung costs about ten times the one above. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Describe the rule for using the ladder.
options: Start at the top and go down only as far as you must — never buy a rung you do not need
Always run a pilot, because only a pilot shows how the idea works at scale
Start at the bottom, because the most expensive test gives the most reliable answer and saves time later
Skip the top rungs, because asking and watching are too informal to count as tests
questions.why: Every rung skipped is real money saved. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Identify what 'ask five people' can settle.
options: Whether the problem is real at all
Whether the effect holds at scale across several branches
Whether it changes behaviour when customers have a real choice
Whether people understand the sign or the form in front of them
questions.why: Five short conversations with real users. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Identify what 'watch them' can settle.
options: What people do rather than say
Whether the effect holds at scale
Whether the problem is real
Whether the pilot works
questions.why: Observe actual behaviour for one shift. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Identify what a pilot can settle.
options: Whether the effect holds at scale
Whether the problem is real
Whether people understand the sign
What people say
questions.why: One branch, one month, measured. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Identify the five lines of the test plan.
options: The question; what you will measure; proceed if; stop if; in between
Who is involved; what happens; where it takes place; when it runs; why it matters
Cost; time; staff; risk; benefit
The idea; the option; the test; the result; the decision
questions.why: This table goes into your report. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Explain why a stop condition matters.
options: A test with no stop condition is a plan you have already committed to, dressed as an experiment
It saves money, because the test can be ended early when it is clearly failing
Clients require a stop condition before they will approve any test
It makes the test shorter, because the team knows when to end it
questions.why: Notice the third line. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Describe the 'in between' line.
options: Adjust one thing and re-run for a few more days
Proceed anyway, because an in-between result is closer to a pass than a fail
Stop anyway, because an in-between result shows the idea is not strong enough
Ask the boss to decide, because the data cannot settle the question
questions.why: Adjust ONE thing. See §8.4 and §8.5.

questions.stem: Explain why the threshold is written before looking at the result.
options: Without it, any result can be read as encouraging — confirmation bias at the last moment
It looks professional in the final report and shows the client that the method was followed throughout the project
It is faster, because the team does not have to debate the result afterwards
Results are secret until the threshold is written, so nobody can leak them
questions.why: Easy to prevent. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Identify the example proceed line in the chapter.
options: At least 15 pre-orders a day by day three
A good number of pre-orders from regular customers
Staff say it works and customers seem to like it
The manager is happy with the way the shelf is being used
questions.why: Numbers, not adjectives. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Identify the four shapes a result can take.
options: Clear pass; clear fail; in between; the test did not really run
Good; bad; mixed; unknown
Yes; no; maybe; ask again later
Pass with conditions; pass without conditions; fail with lessons; fail without lessons
questions.why: Only one is straightforward. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Explain why a clear fail is the most valuable result.
options: It cost three days instead of nine months
It is the most common result, so the team learns to expect it
It ends the project cleanly, so the team can move to the next one
It pleases the client, who sees that the consultant is honest
questions.why: Three days instead of nine months. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Explain why you adjust only one thing when the result is in between.
options: Changing three things at once means you never know which one mattered
It is cheaper to change one thing than to redesign the whole test
The client allows one change before the test has to be approved again
Time is short, and one change can be made before the next day's trial
questions.why: Adjust ONE thing and re-run. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Describe the dangerous fourth shape.
options: The test did not really run — too few users, staff forgot, the week was atypical
A clear pass, because it tempts the team to proceed at once without checking the limits of what was tested
A clear fail, because it tempts the team to abandon an idea that might work
In between, because it tempts the team to change everything at once
questions.why: Say so and run it again; do not read tea leaves. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Explain how a failed test written up honestly is marked.
options: It earns more marks than a vague success — it shows the method worked
It fails the section, because a recommendation needs a tested option behind it
It is ignored, because the marks are for the recommendation, not the test
It is marked the same as no test, because nothing was proved either way
questions.why: Honest failure beats vague success. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Describe what to do when the assumption holds.
options: Proceed to the recommendation, saying what the test covered and did not
Run another test at the next rung of the ladder to be sure before recommending anything
Abandon the option, because a single test is not enough to act on
Stay silent about the test and present the recommendation on its own
questions.why: Proceed, with its limits stated. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Describe what to do when the assumption fails.
options: Return to the option set from chapter 7 and say which option is ruled out and why
Proceed anyway, because the test may have been run on an unusual week
Change the threshold so that the result counts as in between
Hide the result and present the recommendation the client expected
questions.why: Back to the option set. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Describe what to do when the result is partly true under conditions.
options: Recommend with the condition attached, stated as a requirement
Proceed without conditions, because a partial pass is still a pass
Stop, because an option that only works under conditions is too fragile
Re-run until the result is clear one way or the other
questions.why: The condition becomes a requirement. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Describe what to do when nothing usable came out of the test.
options: Re-run, or say honestly it is untested — do not imply otherwise
Claim it passed, because nothing in the result contradicts the recommendation
Claim it failed, because a test that produced nothing cannot support the option
Skip the section, because there is nothing to report
questions.why: Say that it is untested. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Explain what earns marks in section 5 of the report.
options: A recommendation that names what was tested, what the test showed, and what remains uncertain
Certainty, because a client needs a clear answer rather than a list of doubts
A long list of tests, because more testing shows more rigour
A confident tone, because hesitation undermines the recommendation
questions.why: Certainty you have not earned loses credibility. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Identify the cost of the 'paper version' rung.
options: About a day
About an hour
Several weeks
Several months
questions.why: A mock sign, form or menu shown to real users. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Explain why stated intention is weak evidence.
options: People say one thing and do another — watch what they do
People lie on purpose when asked about their intentions
Intentions change daily, so a survey is out of date by the next morning
Surveys are expensive, so the sample is always too small
questions.why: Watch what people DO. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the supermarket's five assumptions. Determine the one in the bottom-right cell.
options: 'Customers will use the self-checkouts' — unsure, and fatal if wrong
'The machines will work with the till system' — fatal if wrong and never checked
'Shrinkage will not rise' — unsure and potentially very costly
'Two cashier posts can be removed' — the whole business case depends on it
questions.why: Unsure + fatal = test first. See Exercise 1 and §8.1.

questions.stem: Classify 'the machines will work with the existing till system'.
options: Fatal if wrong, but IT can confirm it cheaply — not the riskiest
The riskiest assumption, because the whole project fails if the systems do not connect
Small damage and confident, because suppliers always make their systems compatible
Not an assumption, because the supplier has guaranteed compatibility in the contract
questions.why: Confidence is not evidence, but it is checkable fast. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Analyse 'two cashier posts can be removed'. Determine why it is a tempting wrong answer for riskiest.
options: It feels big, but it follows from the usage assumption — test usage first
It is the riskiest, because it is the saving that justifies the whole project
It is unimportant, because staff costs are a small part of the total
It is already proven, because other supermarkets have removed cashiers
questions.why: The usage assumption sits underneath it. See Exercise 1. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Select the single question a test of the riskiest supermarket assumption must answer.
options: 'Will customers actually use the self-checkouts when both options are open?'
'Do customers like the idea of self-checkouts when it is explained to them?'
'Is 300,000 dirhams a fair price for the machines and the installation?'
'Will the finance director approve the project at the next board meeting?'
questions.why: One question, ending in a question mark. See Exercise 1 and §8.2.

questions.stem: Classify an assumption the team is confident about whose failure would cost little.
options: No test — note it and move on
Test first, because every assumption deserves evidence
Pilot, because a pilot settles every assumption at once
Abandon, because an untested assumption is a risk
questions.why: Confident + small: note it. See §8.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the manager's plan: show the concept to twelve regulars in a meeting room and ask if they would use it. Determine the conditions it fails.
options: It measures what people say, has no threshold, and no result would stop him
It fails none of them — twelve regulars are a reasonable sample
Only the threshold is missing; the question and the audience of regulars are right
Only the question is wrong; the method and the threshold are fine
questions.why: Watch what people DO; threshold before; a result that could stop you. See Exercise 2 and §8.2.

questions.stem: Determine what the manager will actually learn from his meeting-room version.
options: Whether twelve polite regulars are willing to say yes to his face
Whether customers will use the machines when they have a real choice
Whether queues will fall once the machines are installed
Whether shrinkage will rise once customers scan their own items
questions.why: They want to be kind. See Exercise 2. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'we will proceed if most say yes'.
options: A threshold that is not a number and measures opinion, not behaviour
A good threshold, because it sets a clear majority rule
A stop condition, because the test ends if most say no
A pilot, because it tests the idea with real customers
questions.why: Numbers, and behaviour. See §8.2 and §8.4.

questions.stem: Select the condition that turns a demonstration into a test.
options: A written result that would make you stop
A bigger audience, so that the result is statistically reliable
A nicer slide, so that the audience understands what is being tested
A longer meeting, so that every objection can be heard
questions.why: If no outcome could change your mind, it is not a test. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Select the highest rung that still answers 'will customers use self-checkouts?'.
options: A one-day trial with borrowed machines, one store
Ask five people whether they would use a self-checkout
A pilot in three stores over a full month
A full installation in one store with the cashiers removed
questions.why: The question is about behaviour; a trial answers it before a pilot. See Exercise 2 and §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the rung for 'is the queue really a problem for customers?'.
options: Ask five people
Pilot in one store for a month
One-day trial with borrowed machines
Paper version of the new checkout layout
questions.why: Whether the problem is real at all. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the rung for 'do customers understand the new self-service sign?'.
options: Paper version
Pilot
Ask five people
One-day trial
questions.why: Whether they understand it. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that goes straight to a one-month pilot for a pre-order shelf. Determine the error.
options: They bought a rung they did not need — a one-day trial could settle it
Nothing — pilots are the most reliable form of test and should always be preferred
The pilot is too short; a shelf needs three months to build a habit
They should ask five people instead of running anything at all
questions.why: Never buy a rung you do not need. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the correctly written proceed line for the Saturday self-checkout trial.
options: 'Proceed if at least 30% of customers with under 10 items choose a machine when a cashier is free'
'Proceed if customers seem happy with the machines at the end of the day'
'Proceed if the machines work without technical problems during the trial'
'Proceed if the store manager is satisfied with how the day went'
questions.why: Numbers, not adjectives. See Exercise 3 and §8.4.

questions.stem: Select the behaviour measure, not the opinion measure, for the trial.
options: Count of customers who choose the machine when a cashier is free
A satisfaction question asked at the exit after the trial
Staff impressions collected at the end of the shift
The supplier's written report on how the machines performed during the day
questions.why: Behaviour rather than opinion. See Exercise 3. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a test plan with a proceed line but no stop line. Determine the problem.
options: It is a commitment dressed as an experiment
Nothing — a proceed line is enough to decide
It needs a bigger sample before the proceed line can be trusted
It needs a pilot rather than a trial to be a real test
questions.why: A test with no stop condition. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Determine what would show the Saturday trial 'did not really run'.
options: Machines down for hours, staff steering everyone to cashiers, or an unusually quiet day
A clear fail, with almost nobody choosing the machines
A clear pass, with most customers choosing the machines
Customers complaining about the machines during the trial
questions.why: The fourth shape. See Exercise 3 and §8.5.

questions.stem: Classify a result of 4 pre-orders a day against stop line 5.
options: Clear fail — the most valuable result, and cheap
Clear pass, because four orders show that customers understood the shelf
In between, because four is close to the stop line of five
Did not run, because four orders is too few to count
questions.why: Below the stop line. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Classify 9 pre-orders a day with proceed 15 and stop 5.
options: In between — adjust one thing and re-run
Clear pass, because nine is well above the stop line
Clear fail, because nine is well below the proceed line
Did not run, because the result is too ambiguous
questions.why: Adjust ONE thing. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that changes the sign, the price and the location after an in-between result. Determine the error.
options: Three changes at once — they will never know which one mattered
Nothing — an in-between result calls for improvement on every front at once
Too few changes — the whole design should be reconsidered
Wrong rung — they should have run a pilot
questions.why: Change one thing. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Determine the right action when only three customers saw the test because staff forgot to point it out.
options: Say it did not really run and run it again
Call it a fail, because three customers is far below any threshold
Call it a pass, because the three who saw it all used it
Average the three and scale the result up to the full day
questions.why: Do not read tea leaves. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Determine the report line when the test passed in one branch only.
options: 'The assumption held in the trial branch; the test did not cover other branches or a full month'
'The assumption is proven everywhere, since customers are the same across branches'
'Untested, because one branch is not enough to count as a test'
'Failed, because the other branches were not included'
questions.why: Say what the test covered and what it did not. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Determine the action when the riskiest assumption fails the test.
options: Return to the chapter 7 option set and say which option is ruled out and why
Proceed with the same option, because one test is not conclusive
Lower the threshold so that the result counts as a pass
Run a pilot anyway, because a pilot gives a more reliable result
questions.why: Back to the option set. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'proceed, on condition that a cashier remains open at peak' after a partly-true result.
options: A recommendation with the condition stated as a requirement
A clear pass, because the option works in the tested situation
A failed test, because the option did not work on its own
An untested recommendation, because the condition was not part of the plan
questions.why: Partly, under conditions. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a report that implies a test passed when nothing usable came out. Determine the verdict.
options: It loses credibility — say honestly it is untested
Acceptable, because the client wants a clear recommendation
Good marketing, because confidence sells the recommendation
Required, because the report must support its recommendation
questions.why: Do not imply otherwise. See §8.6.

questions.stem: Analyse 'shrinkage will not rise'. Determine its cell in the grid.
options: Unsure and serious, but not fatal to the decision — decide and watch it, after the usage test
The riskiest, because theft could wipe out the saving from the cashier posts
Confident and small, because shrinkage is low in this store
Not an assumption, because shrinkage is measured already
questions.why: Rank against the usage assumption. See Exercise 1 and §8.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a test asked of colleagues rather than customers. Determine the flaw.
options: They are not the customer, they want to be kind, and nothing they say could stop you
Colleagues know too much about the business to judge the idea fairly
It is too expensive, because colleagues' time costs the company money
It takes too long to collect opinions from a whole department
questions.why: The classic bad test. See §8.2.

questions.stem: Determine the cost ratio between rungs of the ladder.
options: Each rung costs roughly ten times the one above
Each rung costs about the same as the one above
Each rung is cheaper than the one above
Costs are unknown until the test is run
questions.why: Roughly ten times. See §8.3.

questions.stem: Select the correct stop line for a pre-order shelf test.
options: 'Stop if fewer than 5 pre-orders a day by day three'
'Stop if it feels wrong to the staff running the shelf'
'Stop if the manager says the shelf is not working'
'Never stop — give the shelf time to build a habit'
questions.why: Numbers, set before. See §8.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a group that writes up a failed test honestly. Determine how it is marked.
options: Better than a vague success — the method worked
As a failure, because the recommendation has no tested option
Not marked, because the test did not support the recommendation
The same as no test, because nothing was proved
questions.why: Honest failure earns more. See §8.5.

questions.stem: Determine what must be named in a recommendation after a test.
options: What was tested, what the test showed, and what remains uncertain
Only the good news, because the client wants confidence
The cost of the test and who paid for it
The supplier who provided the equipment for the trial
questions.why: Certainty you have not earned loses credibility. See §8.6.
